← Egress window bid calculator

How much to charge to install an egress window

Foundation and basement contractors get shopped on a published $1,800 egress window installed Facebook special. Those numbers cannot see the cut or the well. A vinyl hopper into an existing hole with a plastic well is a different job from a casement in a new poured-wall cut with a stone well, a drain, a cover, a ladder, and a dirt haul.

Open the free egress window bid calculator

Price the opening and the cut, not the $1,800 dump

An egress window is an opening, then a cut, then a well. Retrofit swaps the sash and the well on a hole that already exists. A wood cut is a header and flashing. Masonry is a saw and a lintel. Poured concrete is a saw, a core, and a lintel. Matching an installed special on a poured-wall new-cut is how a sold legal bedroom becomes a loss when the saw and the haul eat the margin.

Hopper versus casement on the same opening

Homeowners usually start from the hopper special, then ask whether a slider or a casement is “a little more.” On the same opening and the same cut it is not a little more. A slider is the common legal-bedroom sash. A casement is a clearer opening. Fiberglass is weight. The calculator prices all four sashes on the opening you already counted so you can quote the upgrade instead of matching the hopper number on a casement job.

A retrofit is not a poured-wall cut

The cheap special is almost always a hopper into an existing hole, a plastic well, no cover, no drain, no haul. A poured-wall stone-well job is a different crew day. Matching a published installed number on that job is how a sold legal bedroom becomes a loss.

This is not window replacement, basement finishing, or waterproofing

Window replacement is wall openings, united inches, and a nailing flange — no excavation. Basement finishing is framing a rec room. A skylight is a roof cut. Basement waterproofing is an interior drain, wells as a waterproofing add-on, and a sump pit. Foundation repair is piers. This prices an egress window: the opening, the cut, the well, and the extras.

Customer-supplied sash is not a free set

Owners also shop a second special: “I already bought the window — just cut and set it for $1,800.” Zeroing the sash and well invoices drops the bid. The cut and the set stay. A hopper that will not pass is a second trip. See should I install a customer-supplied egress window for the three-way comparison on the same opening. On a typical masonry legal bedroom the owner-supplied walk-away is still above $1,800 even when they bought the kit.

Saturday is not the weekday bid

Owners also call with a weekday number and ask you to start Saturday so the basement can be a legal bedroom before a listing or a school year. After-hours is time-and-a-half plus a second trip — you cannot leave an open foundation hole overnight. On the sample rates a typical masonry legal bedroom prices about $3,976.62 when they leave and $4,990.68 after hours. A $3,500 Saturday number covers the weekday and loses $492.54. See should I cut an egress window on Saturday.

Walk-away price

Load the wage with payroll burden. Add overhead as a share of direct cost. Then take margin as a share of the customer’s price, not a markup on cost. The walk-away number is total cost. A proposed price under that number loses money before you take anything out of it.

This page is a walkthrough of the arithmetic in the egress window bid calculator. It is not a building-code determination, an egress-size approval, a foundation design, a waterproofing design, or a price you should copy onto a contract.

Common questions

How much should I charge to install an egress window?

Charge from window count, sash, cut, well, and extras — not a published $1,800 installed special. A vinyl hopper into an existing hole with a plastic well is a different job from a casement in a new poured-wall cut with a stone well, a drain, a cover, a ladder, and a dirt haul.

Is a retrofit the same bid as a new poured-wall cut?

No. Retrofit swaps the sash and the well on a hole that already exists. A wood cut is a header and flashing. Masonry is a saw and a lintel. Poured concrete is a saw, a core, and a lintel. Matching an installed special on a poured-wall new-cut is how a sold legal bedroom becomes a loss when the saw and the haul eat the margin.

How do the sash, the well, and extras change an egress price?

A vinyl hopper is the cheap-special sash. A slider is the common legal-bedroom sash. A casement is a clearer opening. Fiberglass is weight. Plastic is the cheap well. Steel is projection. Stone is built in place. Cover, ladder, drain, dirt haul, and interior finish do not live in a published installed dump.

Is this the same as window replacement, basement finishing, or waterproofing?

No. Window replacement is wall openings, united inches, and a nailing flange — no excavation. Basement finishing is framing a rec room. A skylight is a roof cut. Basement waterproofing is an interior drain, wells as a waterproofing add-on, and a sump pit. Foundation repair is piers. This prices an egress window: the opening, the cut, the well, and the extras.

    Common questions

    Why can a competitor advertise “$1,800 egress window installed”?

    Usually because the special is written around one specific job, and that job is a preset here: a vinyl hopper retrofit into an existing opening with a plastic well, no cover, ladder, drain, or haul-away. It really does price low. What the flat number cannot see is scope, window type, well material, and every extra. Price your actual basement beside the special and the gap becomes a list of line items instead of an argument about who is honest.

    Why does cutting a new opening in poured concrete cost so much more than a wood-framed wall?

    Because the wall material decides how the opening gets made. Retrofitting an existing opening is the cheapest scope — no new cut at all. A wood-framed wall needs a header and flashing. CMU or block needs a lintel and a saw. Poured concrete needs a concrete saw, coring, and a structural lintel, which is the slowest and most equipment-heavy of the four scopes. Each scope has its own starting hours and material because sawing block and sawing poured concrete are not the same job with a different name.

    Is this the same as a window replacement?

    No. Window replacement swaps glass into an existing wall opening with no excavation. An egress window can require cutting a brand-new opening in the foundation wall and always adds a window well outside — excavation, drainage, and backfill that a straightforward replacement never touches. This tool is also distinct from basement finishing (framing a rec room), a skylight (a roof cut), basement waterproofing (an interior drain and sump pit), and foundation repair (piers).

    Why does the well material matter if the code depth is the same?

    Because plastic, steel, and stone wells are different install jobs, not just different looks. A plastic well is the cheap-special assumption. A steel well projects further from the wall and needs more backfill. A stone or masonry well is built in place, course by course, on site. On top of the well itself, a cover, a ladder, and a drain are each optional add-ons priced separately — code may require some of them depending on well depth, which this calculator does not determine.

    No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. Your bid is saved in this browser’s local storage so it is still here next visit, and the optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your job details, wages, or prices.

    What’s the difference between the bid price and the walk-away price?

    The bid price already includes your target margin on top of labor, materials, and overhead. The walk-away price is the total cost underneath it — the cut, the window, the well, and every extra — the point below which the job stops being profitable at all. Typing a price you are considering shows you the margin or the loss before you send it.

should-i-cut-an-egress-window-on-saturda.text:

Should I cut an egress window on Saturday?

Owners call with a weekday number: “Can you start Saturday? We need the legal bedroom before the listing. Same $3,500?” That sounds like the same opening. It is not the same crew day. After-hours is time-and-a-half. You cannot leave a four-foot foundation hole overnight, so it is a second trip to plate or fence it. Working around a family that still uses the basement on a weekday is the same wage on a slower cut.

Open the free egress window bid calculator

Saturday is not the weekday bid

A weekday they leave still carries the wage you already timed. After-hours raises that wage to time-and-a-half and adds a starting second trip. On a typical masonry legal bedroom — vinyl slider, steel well, cover, drain, ladder, $42 wage, 30% burden, 15% overhead, 20% target margin, 14 miles — the weekday bid is $3,976.62. After-hours is $4,990.68. The walk-away jumps from $3,181.30 to $3,992.54. Taking $3,500 to “just do Saturday at the weekday number” covers the empty weekday and loses $492.54 after hours.

Weekday, they leaveWeekday, they stayAfter-hours / Saturday

At $3,500 Saturday specialCoversCoversLoses $492.54

A poured-wall stone well loses even on the weekday

The Saturday special is more tempting when they already have the $1,800 Facebook number in mind and the wall is poured concrete. The weekday bid is $7,494.94. They-stay-in-the-basement is $7,757.87. After-hours is $9,045.85 and the walk-away is $7,236.68. Taking $1,800 to “just cut what I bought, this weekend” still loses money — even on the weekday.

This is not a customer-supplied sash or a walk-in shower

Customer-supplied kits are their sash and an install-only number — see should I install a customer-supplied egress window. After-hours is when you can stand in the yard and whether the hole stays open overnight. A walk-in shower Saturday is tile overtime in the only bath they still use. A toilet Saturday is an overflowing closet. A boiler Saturday is a no-heat call. This prices an egress window: the opening, the cut, and the well.

How to use the comparison

Open the egress window bid calculator, pick the typical legal-bedroom or losing-job preset, and put their Saturday number in “price you’re considering.” The access table scores that number against a weekday they leave, they-stay-in-the-basement, and after-hours / Saturday. Nothing is uploaded.

This is the same arithmetic as how much to charge to install an egress window. It is not a labor-law determination, a union scale, or a reason to refuse a customer — it is the walk-away number on each access window.

Common questions

Should I cut an egress window after hours or on Saturday?

Only after you price time-and-a-half plus a second trip to plate the hole. You cannot leave an open foundation excavation overnight. A $3,500 Saturday special on a typical masonry legal bedroom covers an empty weekday and loses $492.54 after hours. A $1,800 Facebook special on a poured-wall stone well sits under that walk-away number even on an empty weekday.

Does working around a basement they still use change the bid?

Yes. Same wage, slower cut, set, and punch-list. On a typical masonry slider with a steel well the they-stay bid is $4,163.03 versus $3,976.62 when they leave.

Can I take the weekday $3,500 number on Saturday?

Usually not on the job they actually want. On a typical masonry legal bedroom the after-hours walk-away is $3,992.54. $3,500 covers an empty weekday and loses $492.54 after hours. On a poured-wall stone well, $1,800 still loses money even on the weekday.

← Egress window bid calculator

Should I install a customer-supplied egress window?

Owners call with a hopper in the driveway: “I already bought the window at Menards. Can you just cut and set it for $1,800?” That sounds like free margin because the sash and well invoices left the bid. They did not leave the masonry cut, the drain, the set hours, or the chance that the hopper will not pass a legal-bedroom inspection.

Open the free egress window bid calculator

Zeroing the kit is not a free cut

A contractor-supplied slider still carries the sash and well invoices. An owner-supplied kit that actually fits zeros those lines and keeps the same cut and set hours. On a typical masonry legal bedroom — vinyl slider, new-cut masonry, steel well, cover, drain, ladder, $42 wage, 30% burden, 15% overhead, 20% target margin, 14 miles — the contractor-supplied bid is $3,976.62. Zeroing a $520 sash and a $480 well drops it to $2,539.12, but the owner-supplied walk-away stays at $2,031.30. Taking the Facebook special to “just cut and set what they bought” for $1,800 still loses $231.30.

You supplyThey supply, it fitsThey supply, wrong size
Sash and well invoices in the bidYesNoNo
Cut and set hoursSameSameSame, plus a callback
Your bid$3,976.62$2,539.12$3,569.17
At $1,800 install-onlyLoses $1,381.30Still loses $231.30Loses $1,055.34

Wrong size is a second trip

Store shelves default to a vinyl hopper and a 36-inch plastic well. Plenty of legal bedrooms need a slider or casement for the 5.7 sq ft clear opening, and a well that actually projects. Setting the wrong kit means an exchange or a legal replacement sash. Price that callback on the same opening before you agree. The calculator adds a starting second trip and a vinyl-slider replacement sash on top of the rates you already typed.

The cheap retrofit special is a different job

A hopper into an existing hole with a plastic well can still hold a margin at $1,800, even when you supply the kit. That is the Facebook special. Matching that number on a masonry new-cut — the job that actually makes a basement a legal bedroom — is how a sold opening becomes a loss when the saw and the well eat the margin. The calculator prices both openings on the same wage so you can show the owner the difference.

How to use the comparison

Open the egress window bid calculator, enter the opening you are standing in, and put their install-only number in “price you’re considering.” The who-supplies table scores that number against you-supply, owner-supplies-it-fits, and owner-supplies-wrong-size. Nothing is uploaded.

This is the same arithmetic as how much to charge to install an egress window. They want Saturday? See should I cut an egress window on Saturday. It is not a building-code determination, an egress-size approval, or a reason to refuse a customer — it is the walk-away number on each supply path.

Common questions

Should I install an egress window the customer bought at a store?

Only after you price the cut without the sash and well invoices. Pulling their Menards kit is still a trip, a saw, and crew hours. A $1,800 install-only special often sits under that walk-away number even when the kit is free to you.

Does a customer-supplied egress window make the $1,800 installed special profitable?

Usually not on a legal-bedroom new cut. Zeroing a $520 slider and a $480 steel well drops the bid, but loaded labor, the masonry cut, the drain, travel, and overhead stay. On a typical masonry new-cut the owner-supplied walk-away is still above $1,800. A hopper that will not pass adds a second trip and a legal replacement sash.

What if the store-bought hopper or well will not pass inspection?

That is a second dispatch plus a legal replacement sash or a deeper well. Store hoppers often miss the 5.7 sq ft clear opening, and a 36-inch plastic well often misses the projection. Price that callback on the same opening before you agree to set whatever they rolled into the driveway. The calculator adds a starting callback trip and a vinyl-slider replacement sash on top of your current rates.

vs-a-flat-rate-egress-window-special.htm.text:
← Egress Window Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat "$1,800 installed" egress window special

"$1,800 egress window installed" is not a price for an egress window install — it is a price for one specific opening, one cut, and one well, quietly applied to every basement window the truck pulls up to.

What a flat "$1,800 installed" special is

A flat special is the fastest way to quote: one headline number on a postcard or a website, read off and repeated. Homeowners shop it because it is easy to compare between bids, and it is the number a customer holding a competitor's flyer will ask you to match on their own basement.

The number behind it was set for one job — usually the cheapest opening type (a vinyl hopper retrofit into an existing hole), the cheapest well (plastic), no drain, no cover, no ladder, no haul — and then reused for every egress window afterward, whether or not the next opening looks anything like a retrofit.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the window count and opening type — vinyl hopper, slider, casement, or fiberglass — whether the opening is a retrofit into an existing hole or a new cut in wood-framed wall, CMU/block, or poured concrete, the well (plastic, steel, or stone), extras such as a cover, a ladder, a drain, and a dirt haul, who supplies the sash and well, the schedule, and your loaded labor and overhead. It prices the opening, the cut, the well, and the extras separately, and returns a walk-away price and an extra-work share below which the job loses money — for this opening, not a generic one.

Job$1,800 specialWalk-away priceVerdict
Cheap special: 1 vinyl hopper, retrofit existing opening, plastic well$1,800.00$1,662.19Covers, +$137.81
Typical legal bedroom: 1 vinyl slider, new-cut masonry, steel well, cover, drain, ladder$1,800.00$3,976.62Loses $2,176.62
Losing job: 1 casement, poured-concrete cut, stone well, cover, drain, ladder, haul, interior finish$1,800.00$7,315.25Loses $5,515.25

Worked using this calculator's own starting kits at a $42 crew wage, 30% payroll burden, 15% overhead on direct cost, and a 20% target margin — the form's own defaults, not a number invented for this page. Open the calculator's presets to check any row yourself.

What a flat special doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same headline price whether the job is a vinyl hopper retrofit into an existing hole or a casement in a new poured-concrete cut — several times the labor and material for the same words "egress window". Prices the opening from the entered window type, scope, and well, so the two jobs above come out at different numbers instead of one.
Prices "an egress window" as one drop-in swap, with no separate line for sawing a new opening, setting a deeper well, or hauling the spoil out of the hole. Times the cut, the well, and the haul as their own extra-work hours, so that work shows up instead of being absorbed into the sash price or skipped.
Assumes a plastic well and no drain, cover, or ladder, so a steel or stone well, a sump-tied drain, a safety cover, or an egress ladder gets quoted the same as one that needs none of that. Adds well material, drain, cover, and ladder line items only for what was entered, so the two jobs price differently.
Bakes payroll burden into a round "labor rate" nobody re-derives, so the rate quietly drifts from the crew's real loaded cost. Loads the entered hourly wage by the entered payroll-burden percentage every time, so labor cost tracks the actual burden rather than a memorized rate.
Gives the tech a price to quote, not a number to check a quote against when an owner asks to match a cheaper retrofit quote on a poured-wall new-cut. Reports the walk-away price and the extra-work share of the job, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before the tech commits to it.

A flat special is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one job it was built for, and nothing about a postcard rate tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat "$1,800 installed" egress-window special get the price wrong?

Because the labor and material scale with the opening, the cut, and the well, not with the word "egress window" alone. A vinyl hopper retrofit into an existing hole with a plastic well is a different job from a slider or casement in a new masonry or poured-concrete cut with a steel or stone well, a drain, a cover, a ladder, and a haul. A flat special quotes both the same and is wrong on one of them every time.

What does a flat special usually leave out entirely?

The cut, the well, and the dirt. A published installed price is set on a retrofit — swap the sash and the well, no saw, no new opening — and has nowhere to put the hours for sawing a new opening in masonry or poured concrete, setting a deeper steel or built-in-place stone well, adding a drain, a cover, and a ladder, or hauling the spoil. A tech pricing off the special alone is short before the saw starts.

How much does the cut and the well actually add over the retrofit special?

On this calculator's own worked examples, at a $42 crew wage, 30% burden, 15% overhead, and a 20% target margin: a retrofit hopper into an existing opening with a plastic well walks away at $1,662 — the $1,800 special covers it with room to spare. The same window as a new masonry cut with a steel well, cover, drain, and ladder walks away at $3,977, almost $2,200 over the special. A poured-concrete cut with a stone well and a haul walks away at $7,315, over $5,500 over the special. The cut and the well, not the sash, are what move the number.

Is a flat rate ever the right way to quote an egress window?

For the one job it was actually priced on — a retrofit into an existing opening, a vinyl hopper, a plastic well, no drain, no cover, no ladder, no haul — a flat rate can land close, and on this calculator's own numbers it does. The risk is applying it to a new-cut job without noticing, because the postcard rate does not know which job it is looking at and neither does the tech until the saw is out.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local rates, permit fees, or what competitors charge. It takes the window count, opening type, cut, well, extras, who supplies the sash and well, the schedule, and your loaded labor and overhead, and turns them into a walk-away price and extra-work share for the job you describe — the arithmetic a flat rate skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat "$1,800 installed" special is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest shortcut that works until the job stops matching the one the rate was set on. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it.

Open the Egress Window Bid Calculator and price your own job.

Two different shapes: Jobber is account-based field-service software for running a home-service business's clients, quoting, scheduling, invoicing, and payments. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this egress-window job cost, given its opening type and cut, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

Jobber is field-service management software founded in 2011 and headquartered in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, used by home-service businesses across HVAC, plumbing, electrical, lawn care, and cleaning trades. It combines client management, quoting, scheduling, invoicing, and payment collection into one subscription system meant to run a whole business across every job and every crew, and it says it serves over 200,000 users. It is sold as an ongoing subscription account. Jobber's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — home-service field-service management software, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Jobber appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Jobber does. It does not manage clients, schedule crews, send invoices, or collect payments, and it stores no customer record on a server. It takes one egress-window job — window count, opening type (hopper, slider, casement, fiberglass), whether the opening is a retrofit into an existing hole or a wood, masonry, or poured-concrete cut, well material, extras, who supplies the sash and well, and whether the crew works a weekday, an occupied-basement day, or a Saturday or after-hours call — and turns that into the extra-work share and the walk-away price below which the job loses money, before any of it touches a client or scheduling system. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.
